region: Coastal northern California and southern Oregon, USA
description: Coast redwood is a light, reddish, decay-resistant softwood from coastal California and Oregon. It is used for decking, siding, outdoor furniture, planters, and burl veneer and turning stock.

hazards.summary: IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancer of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long-term heavy exposure. This applies to every species, so dust control matters whatever you cut.
Three workers have been reported with asthma from redwood sawdust, each confirmed by an exposure or inhalation challenge test. The cause is thought to be small chemical compounds in the wood.

'Sequoiosis' is a lung inflammation described in 1967 in people who breathed redwood sawdust. It is often attributed to molds growing on moldy redwood dust rather than the wood itself, but we could not confirm that from the original abstract.

exposure_limits.note: 8-hour time-weighted average, as restated by OSHA

related_species_note: Giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) and dawn redwood (Metasequoia) are different trees. In European timber trade 'redwood' often means Scots pine (see the pine page).
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Light cherry-red to deep reddish-brown heartwood with a narrow strip of pale yellowish-white sapwood along one edge. Straight grain with clearly defined growth rings in alternating lighter and darker bands, coarse open texture, no visible pores, and a soft low luster. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of coast redwood with reddish-brown heartwood, straight banded growth rings and a pale sapwood edge.
notes_internal: Not listed in HSE-WIS30. Goldsmith-1988 (Tier B) was a lead only; primaries cited instead. Cohen-1967 has no PubMed abstract; the mold explanation for sequoiosis (Graphium / Aureobasidium pullulans) is widely repeated but no primary source confirmed in this pass, so the summary hedges. A PubMed search for Graphium/Aureobasidium with redwood found nothing. ACGIH places redwood in A4 'all other wood dusts' (not named). Absence of reports for a hazard is not evidence that this wood is safe.
